title: David Wilkins on globalization, lawyers and emerging economies
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s account of international diffusion through local adaptation rather than convergence on a uniform US model. His India-focused evidence highlights changing US models, distinctively Indian conditions, and the resulting “glocalization,” while also identifying legal education and professional regulation as connected institutional dimensions.
qs: Therefore, Indian law firms and legal departments were simultaneously trying to adopt a model that itself was changing, all the while doing so in relation to distinctively Indian conditions.

What we see emerging is a complex mix of global influences with local adaptations–a process we call “glocalization.”  The third big question that we looked at is how this new corporate sector of the bar influences other sectors of the legal profession, such as legal education and professional regulation.

st.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the synthesis: economic liberalization generated demand for corporate legal services, while Anglo-American models were adapted to distinct Indian institutions rather than producing uniform convergence. He also identifies foreign-firm entry as an ongoing domestic regulatory contest.
qs: What we see emerging is a complex mix of global influences with local adaptations–a process we call “glocalization.”  The third big question that we looked at is how this new corporate sector of the bar influences other sectors of the legal profession, such as legal education and professional regulation.
At the same time, there is a contest about whether foreign law firms that want to come in and serve the Indian market will be allowed to do so.

kp.k: Economic liberalization generated demand for new legal capabilities
kp.d: This February 2018 interview discusses globalization rather than AI. Wilkins links the gradual opening of India, Brazil and China during the 1990s to foreign investment, privatization and competition, which generated demand for new laws, institutions and lawyers able to connect domestic legal fields with global markets.
qs: This new economic activity in turn created a demand for new laws and legal institutions

As a result of these changes, India and other emerging economies have seen the emergence of a new “corporate” legal sector consisting of large law firms and increasingly sophisticated in-house legal departments

kp.k: GLEE investigates corporate lawyers through multidisciplinary empirical research
kp.d: Launched in 2011, GLEE studies the emergence, evolution and wider significance of corporate legal sectors. Wilkins reports more than 50 scholars conducting qualitative and quantitative research on India, China and Brazil, including surveys and interviews with firms, corporate legal departments, educators, public interest advocates and government officials. The Indian volume, published in 2017, draws on twenty empirical studies.
qs: The GLEE project addresses this gap by conducting original quantitative and qualitative research on a broad range of issues surrounding the emergence of a new corporate legal profession in these jurisdictions.
GLEE has administered surveys and conducted interviews with elite firms, in-house legal departments, legal educators, public interest advocates, government officials and others.
Employing a range of original data from twenty empirical studies, it details the emergence of a new corporate legal sector in India

kp.k: Anglo-American organizational models diffused into India's corporate legal sector
kp.d: Wilkins reports substantial evidence of diffusion of large-firm and sophisticated in-house models into India. Many Indian firms had several hundred lawyers, although their resemblance to New York and London firms is qualified as organizational similarity at a surface level. The Indian corporate sector also includes legal process outsourcing companies.
qs: And, we did find substantial evidence that suggests that the model is indeed moving to India.
For example, many Indian law firms now have several hundred lawyers that, at least on a surface level, share many of the same organizational structures as law firms in New York and London.
as well as legal process outsourcing companies.

kp.k: Indian general counsel gained qualifications and organizational standing
kp.d: Drawing on a major study of Indian in-house departments, Wilkins contrasts the period before 2000, when most general counsel reported to the CFO and many lacked law degrees, with the mid-2010s, when the majority reported to the CEO or board and virtually all were qualified attorneys. He presents this as evidence of increasing sophistication and diffusion of the Anglo-American model.
qs: As one example, prior to 2000, most general counsel in India reported to the chief financial officer, and many did not have law degrees.
By the mid-2010s, the majority reported to either the CEO or the board, as in the norm in the United States, and virtually all are fully qualified as attorneys.

kp.k: Local institutions reshape imported organizational models
kp.d: Wilkins describes diffusion as adaptation rather than simple replication. Research found religious, caste, class and regional ties operating within the corporate legal sector; many prominent Indian firms remained family controlled, often connected to similarly controlled business interests. Indian organizations were also adapting to an Anglo-American model that was itself changing, producing what he calls glocalization.
qs: Our research found that these communal ties operate even inside the corporate legal sector.

For example, while most law firms in the United States long ago transitioned from being family owned/controlled businesses, many high-powered, corporate law firms in India are still controlled or dominated by important families.
What we see emerging is a complex mix of global influences with local adaptations–a process we call “glocalization.”

kp.k: Corporate legal growth reshaped education and professional hierarchies
kp.d: Wilkins reports that the Indian studies document effects on legal education, pro bono, corporate social responsibility and gender, communal and professional hierarchies. He specifically connects liberalization and expanding legal needs to growth in national law schools, initially established in the late 1980s, and the establishment of private schools seeking to provide globally oriented legal education.
qs: India created a set of national law schools beginning in the late 1980s that were meant to provide the highest level of training.
With liberalization and the exploding number of legal needs, the number of these law schools has increased dramatically.
the development of pro bono and corporate social responsibility
gender, communal, and professional hierarchies within the bar.

kp.k: Market transformation triggered contests over professional regulation
kp.d: Wilkins describes tensions between India's traditionally restrictive regulation of commercial practices, including advertising, and corporate-sector pressure to relax those restrictions. He separately identifies the contested admission of foreign law firms to the Indian market. These are reported as ongoing conflicts in the 2018 account, not resolved regulatory changes.
qs: Like many countries, regulation in India has traditionally been extremely restrictive around commercial practices, such as advertising.
The new corporate sector has pushed to remove many of these traditional restrictions.
At the same time, there is a contest about whether foreign law firms that want to come in and serve the Indian market will be allowed to do so.

kp.k: Corporate lawyers increasingly influence policymaking and global representation
kp.d: Wilkins reports growing participation by corporate firms and legal departments in Indian legislation, including securities-law negotiations. He also describes investment in corporate legal capacity to represent Indian companies and government in global governance institutions and trade disputes. He qualifies this influence by noting that the corporate sector remains relatively small within the Indian bar.
qs: Thus, when India adopts a new corporate securities law, lawyers from top corporate law firms are increasingly at the negotiating tables.

We also found India investing in the development of the corporate legal sector to build capacity to represent Indian companies and the Indian government in the institutions of global governance, such as the World Trade Organization, or in trade disputes.

Even though the corporate legal sector in India is still relatively small compared to the rest of the Indian bar, its influence in promoting India’s influence in the world has grown quite considerably.

kp.k: Comparative research completion and expansion remained uneven
kp.d: As of the interview, Wilkins reports completed Brazilian research and publication of its book on February 1, 2018. Chinese research completion in the next few months and publication around the same time the following year were prospective. Expansion to Africa was still being planned, with country selection and team formation underway rather than completed research findings.
qs: Our research in China will be completed in the next few months.
The third GLEE book reporting the results of this work will be published by Cambridge University Press around this time next year.
We are now in the process of planning to expand the project to Africa.
Africa, of course, is a continent not a country.

kp.k: Law mediates competing pressures within India's development
kp.d: In the separate Q&A, Vikramaditya Khanna offers the '4 Ds' framework: development, democracy, diversity and demography. He argues that development demands legal change, while electoral accountability and diversity require consensus that can slow reform. A young population creates pressure for faster employment and educational expansion; he cites estimates of nearly 750 million people below 40 and conditionally warns that inadequate opportunities could turn a demographic dividend into disaster.
qs: By some estimates, there are nearly 750 million people in India below the age of 40.
But, of course, if this large population doesn’t have educational and employment opportunities, that demographic dividend may turn into a demographic disaster.

When you look at the 4 Ds of India, the democracy and the diversity of India tend to push towards a more considered, some might say lumbering, development process whereas demography may entail the need for quicker development.
The law and the legal profession in India play a central role in mediating the tensions generated by these powerful forces.

kp.k: Khanna forecasts India's growing economic and geopolitical importance
kp.d: Khanna predicts that India will become a pivotal global player and critical US partner. In this 2018 account, he reports estimates that its population would soon exceed China's and that it would rank among the three largest economies within 15-20 years. These are forecasts rather than observed outcomes; his legal-market argument also emphasizes India's English-speaking common-law system and incomplete openness to international legal competition.
qs: I think India is going to be a pivotal player in the world going into the future, and also a critical partner for the United States going forward.
Most estimates also suggest in the next 15-20 years, India will be among the top three largest economies on the planet.
On top of all of that, India is the largest English speaking, common law jurisdiction in the world.
And it is not yet fully open to global competition in the legal profession.
